description:
Repro (scratch txxd15/p2s.fz): @spec f(integer) :: integer over def f(x), do: x; main receives 1.5 as an any and prints dbg(f(x)). Re-run on fz-rba.4 81dc420d4: interp prints 1.5; run panics 'fz_ref_load_int: ExpectedTag { expected: ValueKind(13), found: ValueKind(14) }' (runtime/src/ir_runtime.rs:237); build not re-run (earlier: same panic). Elixir prints 1.5 (specs are not enforced).
What the docs promise (.agent/docs/specs.md, 'Admission, function'): a function tests its clauses at run time, so a value outside the domain meets the callee's arm of last resort (FunctionClauseError). That holds when the clause itself is typed. Here the clause is untyped, so it has no test, and it admits the float; the caller still reads the call's result as the spec's integer and loads it as a raw int. The three paths disagree because interp carries the value boxed.
The defect is that two readings of one spec are both live: the clause admits what the spec's domain excludes, and the caller trusts the spec's result. Two ways to make them one, and the choice is a language decision for the user:
(a) the spec's parameter domain is a test on an untyped clause when the caller holds any: f(1.5) raises FunctionClauseError on all three paths (matches the specs doc, differs from Elixir);
(b) a spec over an untyped clause does not narrow the result a caller reads for an any argument: f(1.5) is 1.5 on all three paths (matches Elixir, the spec becomes documentation at that call).
Not investigated: where the result type is taken from the contract for an any-keyed callee, and whether a typed argument into the same function is affected.

DECIDED 2026-11-13 by the user (supersedes the earlier 'follow Elixir' decision): ENFORCE, option (a). fz can enforce what Elixir cannot. When a caller cannot prove its argument row inside a function's @spec domain, the spec's parameter domain is tested at run time on entry to a clause that does not test its parameters itself, and a value outside it raises FunctionClauseError on interp, run and build. The spec result is then sound to read. f(1.5) under @spec f(integer) :: integer over def f(x), do: x raises FunctionClauseError. .agent/docs/specs.md 'Admission, function' already states this.
Known consequences to measure, not assume: 482 of 508 lib functions with a @spec have an untested parameter (regex count, scratchpad/i89/count.py), so most library calls with an unproven argument gain an entry test; a lib @spec narrower than what its function does (e.g. @spec concat([a], [a]) over [] ++ x, where Elixir returns x for any x) now raises. Every such case found is reported, not silently re-specced.
The earlier follow-Elixir build (draft PR #527: contract.rs drops the spec result for unproven rows; lib guards in stream.fz, json.fz, string.fz; fixtures 01250/01251 expecting 1.5) is superseded and is replaced on the same branch.

MEASURED 2026-11-13 (run-time enforce build, uncommitted in ../fz-xxd15; patches scratchpad/i89e/i89_full.patch, e1b_*, e2_*): enforcement works on all three paths, but distiller root requests 47,910 -> 68,697 (over the 50,000 budget), 75 failing matrix names. Cause (E1): a spec test is a Region::Type question; demand_for_region (src/dispatch_matrix/mod.rs ~1268) charges it Whole, so recursive lib walkers (List.reduce_cont +142 activations, Enum.map_list +119, ...) are keyed per argument type. A test that does not charge keying needs a new mechanism (a marker through pattern.rs:928, the graph compile and charge_node mod.rs:1161, plus ~8 Region consumers). Testing only untested parameters (E2) changes nothing (68,672). Kernel div/rem's catch-all default (ArithmeticError) becomes unreachable under any run-time reading: Elixir specs are success typings. Open: with '::' leaving patterns (fz-ep5), guards are the only run-time domain; candidate answer is a compile-time check that a clause admitting values outside its @spec can only raise for them (unspiked).

DECIDED 2026-11-13 by the user: a @spec written above a clause is that clause's contract. It states what the clause returns for the arguments it describes, and it is checked at compile time. Guards and patterns pick the clause; a spec never changes which clause runs, as in Elixir. Clause order supplies negation, so a later clause's spec covers only what earlier clauses refused: @spec is_integer(integer) :: true above the first clause, @spec is_integer(term) :: false above the fallback. For fz-i89 this replaces run-time enforcement: a clause that admits values outside its own spec must only be able to raise for them (Kernel div/rem's catch-all passes; 'def f(x), do: x' under @spec f(integer) :: integer is a compile error naming the guard to add). Unspiked.

Widened 2026-11-24 (user): a caller trusts only a spec result that something proved. Second live case, from Bugs and Cleanup: List.concat is declared @spec concat([a], [a]) :: [a], but concat([], 2) returns 2. opaque([1]) ++ opaque(2): interp gives [1 | 2]; run and build exit 139 (SIGSEGV), because native code takes the declared [a] result, writes the outer cons inline with no tail check and stores a scalar where a list address belongs. With experimental specs, [a] | b makes run print 1; a spec without | b makes run and build print [1, #slot<0x2:0>]. fz-sc8.22.3 corrects concat's spec, which removes that case; the hazard remains for any other spec its body does not satisfy. Probes: Bugs and Cleanup scratchpad s22/r3/p/. Options: (a)/(b) above, or fz-p8p.23 (check each body against its own @spec) so a trusted result is a proven one.
title: [BUG] A caller trusts only a @spec result that something proved
